title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that isolates the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair layer (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) relative to accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and validator, we sampled K=200 paired intents and produced a single shared generator output per intent (shared_initial_generation) that was evaluated under two conditions: baseline (accept) and guarded (verify then optionally repair). Requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...). Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked (repair_applied = 0 for all guarded episodes). We release the preregistration (SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...), raw model/provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...), and analysis artifacts to enable exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling effect for this task/model/validator regime, and we discuss design choices required to empirically demonstrate verifier/repair benefit in future confirmatory evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a central NetOps automation use case that promises faster, lower‑effort changes but carries substantial operational risk: incorrect command order or omitted preconditions can cause reachability regressions or outages. A common mitigation pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks functional and workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown‑before‑MTU), and an automated repair step attempts constrained corrections when the verifier fails. Prior systems and benchmarks argue that G→V→R reduces regression risk, but those claims often conflate generator variability, selective reporting, and varying validator coverage.
To produce a clean, reproducible estimate of the verifier’s marginal effect we preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop). The core design choice — shared_initial_generation per task — holds the generator output identical across arms so the only operational difference is the presence of the verifier and the permitted repair invocation. This isolates verifier marginal effect from generator stochasticity and from post‑hoc prompt tuning. Our preregistration, sampling, execution, and analysis were archived and hashed; key artifacts and SHA‑256 values are recorded in the execution manifest and are referenced throughout the paper.
Research question. Under a deterministic task pool and a deterministic validator, does inserting an automated verifier+repair step reduce the incidence of regression‑causing changes relative to accepting an LLM suggestion directly? The confirmatory (primary) hypothesis H1 was that the G→V→R pipeline would yield a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only pipeline (paired estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline).
sections.related_work: LLM assistance for NetOps and AIOps spans intent translation, configuration synthesis, and closed‑loop agentic workflows that incorporate validators and repairers. Recent domain benchmarks and pipelines (generate→validate→repair style) use formal or emulated validators to assess regressions and demonstrate that verifier‑guided iterative workflows can reduce regressions in failure‑rich settings. Position works also emphasise restricting LLMs to translation or model construction while relying on deterministic solvers for long‑horizon reasoning and safety. Our experiment complements that literature by preregistering a strict paired protocol and publishing the full artifact chain so the marginal effect of the verifier can be audited independently of generator variability. The study draws its practical motivation from the growing literature on verifier‑augmented NetOps (e.g., pinned generate→validate→repair benchmarks and recent system prototypes) and from discussions recommending verifier‑first design for operationally risky changes. We explicitly verified closest leads and included their identifiers in the evidence bundle to ensure accurate positioning (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory framing. The complete preregistered experimental plan (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622) froze: (i) the sampling and inclusion rules; (ii) model/provider configuration; (iii) validator semantics and repair policy; (iv) primary estimand and statistical test; and (v) analysis bootstrap parameters (seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Power planning: we targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.08 assuming a baseline regression rate ≈0.20 (two‑sided α=0.05, power=0.80). The preregistration also enumerated exclusion rules (automatic if verifier lacked coverage) and a contamination detection plan (intent hashing and per‑call traces) documented in the execution manifest.
Task pool, deterministic sampling, and inclusion filtering. Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. To avoid human selection bias we implemented a strict deterministic selection pipeline: (1) assemble candidate intents from the public generator outputs; (2) filter to intents where the preregistered validator reported coverage; (3) compute SHA‑256(intent_string) and sort ascending; (4) select the first K=200 tasks. This deterministic selection and the recorded seeds guarantee bit‑exact replay of the task_manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7...). Each manifest entry records initial_state, expected_final_state, the required_sequence of commands, and difficulty diagnostics used by the validator.
Paired shared initial generation protocol. For each of the K=200 tasks we executed a single shared generator call (shared_initial_generation) that produced candidate_c and its provider trace; that single candidate served both arms. The baseline arm treated candidate_c as the LLM suggestion to accept. The guarded arm ran deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on candidate_c and, if the validator flagged violations, was allowed one preregistered repair invocation (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This paired design isolates the verifier’s marginal effect by holding generator output fixed across arms and by preventing generator adaptation to validator feedback during the paired comparison.
Model, provider, and execution bookkeeping. The requested_model was gpt-5-mini and the execution/model_configuration.json artifact captures exact model metadata (SHA‑256 = 1acce92558ed...). All provider call traces for the shared_initial_generation stage are archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json with per‑call hashes; execution/execution_manifest.json contains a full list of artifact hashes (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...). The adapter_family used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the run executed in scientific_confirmatory mode. Provider call auditing tracked hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, and detected no cross‑condition cache reuse (deterministic_reconciliation.json).
Validator semantics, scoring rule, and repair policy. The verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parses candidate text into structured commands and enforces workflow invariants and dependency rules encoded in the validator (examples: shutdown before MTU change; make‑before‑break for uplinks; at least one uplink up). Each scoring trace records normalized_configuration, required_command_count, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshot, violation_codes, and a valid boolean. When valid==false the preregistered repair policy permitted a single constrained repair prompt to the same model, followed by a single revalidation. All scoring artifacts are archived under execution/scoring/*.json and are included in the results manifest.
Confirmatory analysis. The primary confirmatory analysis was the paired binary comparison (validator.valid for baseline vs guarded). We used the exact McNemar two‑sided test for inference and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples and seed=1729 as preregistered. Secondary estimands — time to deploy and model calls per successful apply — were collected but remained uninformative because no repairs occurred.
sections.results:
Execution and provenance. The run completed as preregistered: planned episodes = 400 (2×K), completed episodes = 400, failed episodes = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (one shared generation per task). Key artifact hashes: raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4233332164d0453e2aecdb34d52a01883358d67ac30e028e6; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa; master prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The full execution manifest enumerates every artifact and hash for reproducibility.
Primary confirmatory outcome. Observed paired counts: complete_pairs = 200; baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200. Paired contingency table (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 7bc1bd2a...). The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. All per‑task scoring traces show validator.valid == true and validator.violation_count == 0.
Repair pathway and operational cost. The guarded repair pathway was never invoked (repair_applied=false across execution/scoring/*.json). Consequently, the guarded arm did not incur additional model calls beyond the single shared generation per task; provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200. Representative per‑task diagnostics (examples in execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) show parsed_command_count and observed_touched_field_count consistent with medium/hard difficulty labels but with final_state snapshots satisfying intent constraints.
Representative task diagnostics. The archived representative_tasks entries (e.g., task-000001) demonstrate artifact grounding: task-000001 required_sequence = [shutdown edge1, set mtu, set vlan, restore edge1], parsed_command_count = 4, observed_touched_field_count = 3, and the normalized_configuration matches the validator final_state. These traces substantiate that the validator exercised nontrivial checks even when candidates passed. Full traces for 200 tasks are archived in execution/scoring and execution/responses with SHA‑256s recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling effect vs practical regimes. The observed degenerate null — perfect validator compliance in both arms — is an informative ceiling case. Under our deterministic task pool, requested_model, and deterministic validator, the generator proposals satisfied all preregistered validator constraints; therefore the verifier had no opportunity to change the binary apply outcome and no repair was required. This shows that, in benign generator/task regimes, the marginal safety benefit of a verifier+repair layer (as instantiated) can be zero. Importantly, this finding does not imply that verifiers are unnecessary in production: operational distributions include vendor quirks, stateful device behavior, obscure dependencies, and historical failure modes that were not present in our synthetic, validator‑covered sample.
Design guidance for future confirmatory evaluations. To demonstrate verifier or repair benefit in confirmatory, preregistered settings one must engineer a failure‑rich evaluation design. Practical design levers (supported by our artifacts) include: (1) sample tasks that deliberately probe validator boundary conditions or include historical failure cases; (2) evaluate weaker or multiple generator models to produce a nonzero baseline error rate; (3) include adversarial or perturbed generator outputs forcing verifier engagement; or (4) change the estimand and design to an interactive generator–verifier loop that allows generator adaptation to verifier feedback. Our shared_initial_generation design intentionally isolates verifier marginal effect but forbids generator adaptation; different design choices probe different operational questions (marginal verifier value vs end‑to‑end interactive workflows).
Statistical and power lessons. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline error ≈ 0.20 and targeted an absolute paired effect of 0.08. Observed baseline = 1.0 invalidated those power assumptions and made demonstrating a reduction impossible: when baseline is degenerate, the paired difference is necessarily zero and null tests are uninformative about verifier efficacy in error‑rich regimes. We therefore report exact tests and bootstrap CIs and avoid post‑hoc power reinterpretation. The analysis artifacts (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and paired_contingency_table.csv) record the exact inferential computations and seeds.
Threats to validity. Internal validity is strong: deterministic sampling, frozen seeds, and cryptographic hashing of all artifacts (execution manifest) eliminate many researcher degrees of freedom. Construct validity depends on the validator’s fidelity: our primary outcome measured validator.valid (a deterministic proxy for regression avoidance), so generalization to true operational regressions depends on validator coverage of real failure modes. External validity is limited by single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and the fact that the shared_initial_generation design prevented generator adaptation. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power target was not met because assumptions were violated by observed baseline; however the exactness of execution and analysis enables trustworthy reporting of the observed ceiling case.
Operational implications. Practitioners should treat this result as a caution: a verifier may be redundant in low‑risk, well‑covered task/model regimes, but production distributions are rarely so benign. A reproducible evaluation contract should (i) document task sampling, (ii) include a diverse failure bank, and (iii) report per‑task validator diagnostics (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, final_state snapshots) — all of which we archive here to demonstrate correct reporting practice and to enable independent replay.
Reproducibility and artifact use. We released the full artifact chain with immutable hashes to enable exact replay: master_prompt provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba; preregistration SHA‑256 = a6d73a5cc0bda22e691a3634068a881b36ae274a65ab33919a647ec32c56e622; raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6580c9df4233332164d0453e2aecdb34d52a01883358d67ac30e028e6; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa; task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = f1d447b7621f83208298f5c8d965bcdbba115e741f95a1efb92944347b35bbf0. Researchers can reproduce: (i) deterministic selection of K=200 tasks from the generator; (ii) shared_initial_generation using the archived provider call traces; and (iii) verifier replay using execution/scoring JSON traces. The deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms internal accounting and provider call audit consistency.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, paired, artifact‑grounded evaluation comparing G→V→R against LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks and found no marginal verifier benefit: both arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair step was never invoked. This is an explicit ceiling case: under the selected task/model/validator regime the generator produced verifier‑compliant candidates and thus the verifier could not alter the binary outcome. For future confirmatory work that aims to quantify verifier/repair utility, evaluators must select failure‑rich task distributions or permit interactive generator–verifier workflows that allow the generator to receive and act on verifier feedback. We publish complete artifacts and hashes to enable exact replay and to support the design of future preregistered evaluations that probe verifier value in operationally realistic settings.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
